claims.text: High configurational entropy is the primary factor stabilizing high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperatures.
High configurational entropy reduces atomic mobility in nanoalloys.
Reduced atomic mobility inhibits diffusion-driven phase separation and chemical segregation.
The initial nanoparticles are uniform, single-phase nanoalloys containing at least five elements with homogeneous constituent distributions.
High configurational entropy provides atomic-scale chemical ordering and a near-uniform elemental distribution.
High mixing entropy decreases the free-energy sensitivity of the nanoalloy to small compositional inhomogeneities.
Decreased free-energy sensitivity to compositional inhomogeneities reduces the driving force for atomic diffusion.
Decreased free-energy sensitivity to compositional inhomogeneities reduces the driving force for phase segregation.
The reduced driving force maintains chemical homogeneity when the temperature is high enough to promote atomic motion.
After high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain a single-phase structure.
After high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will show minimal elemental segregation and minimal intermetallic-phase formation.
Under identical conditions, a lower-entropy binary nanoalloy will undergo more phase separation than the high-entropy nanoalloy.
Under identical conditions, a lower-entropy binary nanoalloy will develop greater chemical heterogeneity than the high-entropy nanoalloy.
Nanoalloys with fewer constituent elements have lower configurational entropy than the proposed high-entropy nanoalloys.
The prediction is limited to nanoscale particles for which surface effects are significant and to temperatures sufficiently below the melting point.
The predicted behavior may change at ultra-long exposure times or at temperatures near the melting range.
The magnitude of stabilization depends on elemental combination and particle-size distribution.
